title: What's for Lunch Around the World?
bigQuestion: How do food and clothes show where a family comes from?

story.title: Five Kinds of Bread
story.kicker: One lunch table holds bread from five places.
paragraphs: It is lunch time in Room 12. Ms. Ruiz says, "Today we share bread from home." Each child opens a lunch box. Everyone looks at the table.
Mateo has a warm corn tortilla. Lina has soft, flat injera. It has tiny holes like a sponge. Ben has a long French bread. Priya has round naan. Mei has a white steamed bun.
The children take small bites. Mateo tries the steamed bun. "It is soft like a pillow!" he says. Lina shows how to tear injera with her fingers.
Ms. Ruiz smiles. "Five breads, five families," she says. "Every one is made with care." The children say thank you to each other.
story.think: What bread or food does your family make or eat a lot? How would you share it?

lessons.title: Rice and Tortillas
lessons.mainIdea: Many families in Asia eat rice, and many families in Mexico eat corn tortillas.
reading: Rice is a small grain. It grows in wet fields. Many families in China, India and Japan eat rice every day.
In Mexico, many families eat *tortillas*. A tortilla is a flat, round bread. It is made from corn. People fill tortillas with beans, meat or cheese.
Rice and tortillas are *staple foods*. A staple food is a food people eat again and again. It helps fill you up.

words.d: a flat, round bread made from corn or wheat
a main food that people eat very often

look.title: Food for Everyone
look.text: Every person has a right to enough food and clothes to stay healthy.
look.cite: United Nations, Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 25, 1948 (simple words)
look.prompt: Why do you think food and clothes are on this list?

check.q: What is a tortilla made from in Mexico?
check.why: The reading says a tortilla in Mexico is made from corn.

check.q: Where do many families eat rice every day?
check.why: The reading names China, India and Japan as places where many families eat rice.

check.q: What is a staple food?
choices: a food for one party only
a main food people eat again and again
check.why: A staple food is a main food people eat very often.

lessons.title: Bread and Injera
lessons.mainIdea: Many families in Europe eat bread, and many families in Ethiopia eat injera.
reading: Bread is made from wheat flour and water. In France, a long bread is called a baguette. In Germany, many families eat dark rye bread.
In Ethiopia, many families eat *injera*. Injera is a big, soft, flat bread. It is made from a tiny grain called *teff*. It tastes a little sour.
Food goes right on top of the injera. People tear off a piece. They use it to scoop up the food.

words.d: a soft, flat bread from Ethiopia with tiny holes
a tiny grain used to make injera

look.title: A Big Round Plate
look.text: Look at a big round injera on a tray. Red lentils sit on one side. Green beans sit on the other side. Two friends tear off pieces. They scoop up the food together.
look.prompt: How is injera like a plate and a spoon at the same time?

check.q: What grain is injera made from?
check.why: The reading says injera is made from a tiny grain called teff.

check.q: What is a long French bread called?
check.why: The reading says a long bread in France is called a baguette.

check.q: How do people eat food on injera?
choices: They tear off a piece and scoop the food.
They cook it in soup first.
check.why: People tear off a piece of injera and use it to scoop up the food.

lessons.title: Chopsticks and Forks
lessons.mainIdea: Many people in East Asia eat with chopsticks, and many people in Europe eat with forks.
reading: *Chopsticks* are two thin sticks. You hold them in one hand. Many families in China, Japan, Korea and Vietnam use them.
A *fork* has sharp points. Many families in Europe and the Americas eat with a fork and a knife.
Both tools help people pick up food. Chopsticks pinch the food. A fork pokes the food. Each one takes practice.

words.d: two thin sticks held in one hand to pick up food
an eating tool with points that pokes food

look.title: Two Bowls of Noodles
look.text: Look at two bowls of noodles. One girl lifts her noodles with chopsticks. One boy twirls his noodles on a fork. Both of them are smiling. Both of them are eating.
look.prompt: Which tool would you like to try? What would help you learn it?

check.q: How do chopsticks pick up food?
choices: They scoop it like a cup.
check.why: The reading says chopsticks pinch the food.

check.q: Which place is one where many families use chopsticks?
check.why: The reading names China, Japan, Korea and Vietnam.

check.q: What do chopsticks and forks both do?
choices: They help people pick up food.
check.why: Both are tools that help people pick up food.

lessons.title: Eating With the Hand
lessons.mainIdea: In many places, people eat with the right hand, and it is polite and clean.
reading: In India, Ethiopia and many other places, people often eat with the hand. They use the right hand. They wash their hands first.
The fingers mix rice and sauce into a small bite. Many people say food tastes better this way. It is a *custom*. A custom is a way a group does things for a long time.
Every custom has *manners*. Manners are kind ways to act. At many tables, you wait for others to start.

words.d: a way a group of people has done something for a long time
kind and polite ways to act with other people

look.title: Wash, Then Eat
look.text: Look at a family in India. Each person washes at the sink. They sit down. A plate of rice and dal sits in front of them. Grandma takes the first bite with her right hand.
look.prompt: What did this family do before eating? Why is that a good idea?

check.q: What do people do before eating with the hand?
check.why: The reading says people wash their hands first.

check.q: What is a custom?
choices: a way a group has done things for a long time
check.why: A custom is a way a group of people does things for a long time.

check.q: Which hand do people often eat with in India?
check.why: The reading says people use the right hand to eat.

lessons.title: Clothes for Hot and Cold
lessons.mainIdea: People wear clothes that fit the weather where they live.
reading: In hot places, people wear light, loose clothes. Loose clothes let air move. A wide hat keeps the sun off your face.
In cold places, people wear thick coats, hats and boots. The Inuit in the far north made warm coats from animal fur. These coats are called *parkas*.
Clothes help keep our bodies safe. They fit the *weather*. Weather is how hot, cold, wet or dry it is outside.

words.d: how hot, cold, wet or dry it is outside
a warm coat with a hood, made long ago by Arctic peoples like the Inuit

look.title: Two Children, Two Places
look.text: Look at two children. One stands in the hot sun. She wears a thin cotton shirt and a wide hat. One stands in the snow. He wears a thick coat with a hood, mittens and boots.
look.prompt: What clothes would you wear in Chicago in January? What about July?

check.q: What kind of clothes do people wear in hot places?
check.why: The reading says light, loose clothes let air move in hot places.

check.q: Who made warm fur coats called parkas in the far north?
check.why: The reading says the Inuit in the far north made parkas.

check.q: What is weather?
choices: how hot, cold, wet or dry it is outside
check.why: Weather is how hot, cold, wet or dry it is outside.

lessons.title: Clothes for Special Days
lessons.mainIdea: Many cultures have special clothes that people wear with pride on special days.
reading: In Japan, some people wear a *kimono* on special days. A kimono is a long robe with wide sleeves. A wide sash ties around the middle.
In India, many women wear a *sari*. It is one long cloth wrapped around the body. In Germany and Austria, some people wear a dress called a dirndl for festivals.
In Guatemala and southern Mexico, many Maya women wear a huipil. It is a woven top with bright designs. Each design can show the wearer's home town.

words.d: a long robe with wide sleeves from Japan
one long cloth wrapped as a dress, worn in India and nearby lands

look.title: A Woven Top
look.text: Look at a huipil on a table. It is red, blue and yellow. It has birds and flowers woven into it. A grandmother wove it by hand. It took her many weeks.
look.prompt: Why might a family keep a huipil for a long, long time?

check.q: What is a sari?
choices: one long cloth wrapped around the body
check.why: The reading says a sari is one long cloth wrapped around the body.

check.q: Where do some people wear a kimono?
check.why: The kimono comes from Japan.

check.q: What can a huipil design show?
check.why: The reading says each huipil design can show the wearer's home town.

lessons.title: Trying New Food Kindly
lessons.mainIdea: When we try a new food, we can take a small bite and use kind words.
reading: A friend may bring a food you have never seen. That is a chance to learn. You can ask, "What is it called?"
You can take a small bite. If you do not like it, that is okay. You can say, "No, thank you." You do not say "yuck."
Being *respectful* means treating people and their food with care. Food is part of a family's culture. Kind words help everyone feel welcome.

words.d: treating people and the things they care about with kindness

look.title: A New Snack
look.text: Look at Sam. His friend Aya brings rice balls wrapped in seaweed. Sam has never tried seaweed. He asks, "What is it called?" Aya says, "Onigiri." Sam takes a small bite.
look.prompt: What could Sam say if he likes it? What could he say if he does not?

check.q: What is a kind thing to say if you do not like a new food?
check.why: The reading says you can say "No, thank you" and not "yuck."

check.q: What can you ask about a new food?
check.why: The reading says you can ask what the food is called.

check.q: What does respectful mean?
choices: treating people and their things with care
check.why: Respectful means treating people and what they care about with kindness.

review.q: Which food is a flat corn bread from Mexico?
review.why: A tortilla is a flat, round bread made from corn in Mexico.
Injera is a soft, flat bread from Ethiopia.

review.q: What do chopsticks and a fork have in common?
choices: Both are worn on special days.
Both help people pick up food.
review.why: Chopsticks and forks are both eating tools.

review.q: Why do people wear parkas in the far north?
choices: to stay warm in the cold
to stay cool in the sun
review.why: Parkas are warm coats for cold places.

review.q: Which is special clothing from Japan?
review.why: The kimono is from Japan. The huipil is Maya, and the dirndl is from Germany and Austria.

review.q: A friend shares a new food. What is a kind thing to do?
choices: Ask its name and try a small bite.
review.why: The chapter says to ask what it is called, try a small bite, and use kind words.
